title: inference-ops-buyer-personas-and-attack-plan
content:
Purpose:
This note is a compact buyer/persona-driven briefing + tactical sales attack plan for conversations where prospects are evaluating managed Redwood Inference versus assembling their own stack using vLLM / Transformers-Glue (TGI) / TensorRT-LLM style components. Focus: practical objections, economic levers, and quick comparison heuristics that SDRs, AEs, and SEs can use in discovery and demo flows.

Top-level thesis (one-liner):
Customers choose self-hosted stacks when they believe they can control unit cost or need absolute customization; they choose Redwood when they want predictable latency/SLOs, lower operational overhead, and cost-controls that scale without hiring a new infra team. Our messaging should move conversations from "can we run it ourselves cheaper?" to "what is the total predictable cost and risk of doing it ourselves over 12–24 months?"

Primary buyer personas and key signals
1) Platform / Infra Engineer (infrastructure owner)
- Signals: control over cloud credits, cares about autoscaling, GPU utilization dashboards, wants IaC + K8s integration.
- Self-host appeal: full kernel-level control, custom scheduler, existing infra incentives.
- Redwood counterplay: emphasize managed autoscaling with burst capacity, tracer hooks for tracing, and predictable throughput commitments; show how Redwood reduces toil (no patching, CVE surface from runtime kernels).

2) ML Engineer / Model Ops
- Signals: cares about model fidelity, token-level debug, KV cache behavior, quantized model variants.
- Self-host appeal: freedom to drop experimental kernels, custom quantization profiles, direct model code changes.
- Redwood counterplay: highlight model catalog, verified performance profiles, fast rollback/rollout controls, and integrated eval hooks to detect quality regressions post-rollout.

3) Product Manager / Application Owner
- Signals: cares about UX latency, cost per MAU, and feature velocity.
- Self-host appeal: perceived lower per-token cost if infra is already owned.
- Redwood counterplay: frame predictable pricing, cost-aware knobs (batching, caching), and fallbacks that preserve SLAs during traffic spikes. Show sample ROI.

4) CTO / Head of Engineering
- Signals: risk, headcount, compliance, long-term TCO.
- Self-host appeal: strategic control and perceived IP.
- Redwood counterplay: emphasize tradeoffs — staff/ops cost and risk of degraded availability, longer time-to-market. Provide headcount-equivalent savings and escalation playbook.

Competitive snapshot: vLLM vs TGI vs TensorRT-LLM (practical view)
- vLLM (open-source batching-focused runtime):
  Strengths: aggressive batching improvements (higher throughput), good for throughput-first workloads where latency SLOs are loose.
  Weaknesses: operational complexity for edge cases (KV cache invalidation across nodes), slower on small-batch low-latency requirements, limited SLAs.
  When good: internal inference pipelines where throughput beats latency and org is comfortable running containerized clusters.

- TGI-style stacks (Transformers + custom adapters + Triton wrappers):
  Strengths: flexible, easy to hack on; good for research/experimentation and custom tokenization or adapters.
  Weaknesses: glue code complexity, manual ops for scaling, inconsistent performance across hardware, and tricky production hardening (retries, fallbacks, A/B rollouts).
  When good: experimentation environments, research teams, and early proof-of-concept phases.

- TensorRT-LLM / vendor-optimized kernels (NVIDIA optimized):
  Strengths: best-in-class latency and throughput for supported models and hardware; excellent in tightly controlled on-prem setups.
  Weaknesses: vendor lock-in, heavy engineering effort for SLOs across mixed fleets, licensing/compatibility issues, and hard to adapt quickly to new model families.
  When good: latency-critical high-volume inference with the budget for deep HW engineering.

How Redwood stacks up (practical messages to use)
- Predictable SLAs: "We commit to latency SLOs and fallbacks — if your primary model variant has a hiccup, requests failover to a compatible variant automatically."
- Unit economics transparency: show per-route token cost, and the levers (batch size, cache TTL, quant profile) that slide cost vs quality.
- Ops reduction: customers move 2–3 FTEs of daily cluster toil to higher-value work within 6–9 months; we use testimonials and a simple headcount ROI calculator in the demo.
- Hybrid flexibility: Same API across hosted / dedicated / private so customers can migrate without rework.

Quick ROI example (talking numbers for enterprise convo)
- Assumptions (example workload): 50M tokens/day, 90% generation, average 20 tokens per request, 300 TPS peak, 5ms target p50 token latency.
- Self-hosted estimate (conservative): requires 8–12 A100-equivalent GPUs for steady-state, 3–4 SRE/infra FTEs, license/maintenance cost for optimized kernels, additional buffer for peak.
- Redwood hosted: predictable monthly usage + optional dedicated nodes for peak, single point billing, integrated cost dashboards.
- Buyer argument: If hiring + infra ops + opportunity cost > ~40% of the managed bill, then managed becomes compelling. Use our headcount x salary calc: 3 FTEs * 160k = 480k/year vs managed delta of ~200–300k/year = net saving + faster feature velocity.

Operational risk matrix (to use in exec conversations)
- Failure modes: model regression after quantization, KV cache invalidation, autoscaler misconfig, noisy neighbor GPU contention when using shared infra.
- Severity: can range from degraded outputs (low business risk) to multi-hour downtime (high business risk).
- Redwood mitigations: integrated evals, canary rollouts, multi-variant fallback, reserved capacity and SLAs.

Sales objection handling (script snippets)
- "We have cloud credits / free infra": Ask about sustained throughput and SRE allocation; translate credits into coverage months and residual ops headcount.
- "We only need latency, not features": Ask about 99th percentile tail and burst patterns; offer short perf benchmark comparing their target model on Redwood vs self-hosted (data-backed).
- "We need total customization": Offer private deployment pitch + workback on how policy/config overrides are delivered via Redwood's private package; highlight audit/KMS integrations.

Technical trial playbook (for SEs)
1) 2-week perf/proof-of-concept: onboard model snapshot, run a 72-hr ramp with synthetic traffic (we provide driver).
2) Key deliverables: per-token latency distribution, cost-per-1M-tokens, cache hit rate, and a failure-injection report.
3) Success criteria: meets p50/p95 targets and demonstrates at least 30% lower ops time during trial.

One-pager attack cards (for SDRs/AEs)
- Low-latency app: pitch = "predictable p95 latency + burst safety nets"; metric to cite = p95 token latency, multi-region failover.
- Cost-sensitive startup: pitch = "smart batching & caching to reduce per-token spend without sacrificing latency"; metric = estimated cost reduction from cache alone.
- Regulated enterprise: pitch = "private deployment + KMS/HSM + audit logs"; metric = time-to-compliance and reduced audit friction.

Action items for GTM content/repos
- Create a one-click microbenchmark repo that runs a customer's public model (Llama-like family) across: vLLM container, TGI baseline, and Redwood hosted endpoint and outputs a clear CSV of latency/throughput/ops assumptions. (Owner: SE team)
- Build a short ROI calculator sheet that reps can use in discovery (inputs: tokens/day, percent generate, desired latency, current infra costs). (Owner: GTM data analyst)

Appendix: short checklist for discovery calls
- What is your p50/p95 target (tokens or request-level)?
- Current steady-state tokens/day and peak TPS?
- Which models and model families are you evaluating and are they quantized?
- Do you have strict data residency/compliance needs?
- How many FTEs currently touch the inference infra?
- Can you share a recent incident postmortem for inference downtime?

Closing note:
This doc should be used as a rapid-reference during discovery and demo prep. Aim to translate technical objections into business metrics (headcount, incident time, SLA risk, and predictable unit cost). Over time we should populate the microbenchmark repo and the ROI sheet with real anonymized customer data to make these conversations more empirical.
